synopsis: Riemann-1.0 uses one transformer backbone to predict an action chunk from interaction history and then predict its visual consequences. During robot deployment, actual observations supply the next context; the policy does not need to generate future video before acting. A separate operating mode generates action-conditioned visual rollouts. Pretraining progresses from latent actions inferred from human videos to mixed trajectory supervision and finally robot-only demonstrations. Reported robot and simulation results are strong, but the paper provides no ablation isolating this curriculum or causal ordering, and its visual-simulator evidence is qualitative. [E03, E07–E09, E11, E13–E17]

problem.text: The authors address how to learn executable robot control from heterogeneous human videos, handheld demonstrations, and robot trajectories while retaining action-conditioned visual prediction. These sources differ in action semantics, temporal resolution, and supervision quality; the proposed solution combines a standardized trajectory interface with action-before-observation causal modeling.

contributions.text: A shared transformer with embodiment-specific interfaces implements both history-conditioned action prediction and action-conditioned visual prediction through an autoregressive factorization.

A three-stage curriculum progressively replaces video-derived pseudo actions with trajectory supervision and increases the action-loss weight, aiming to transfer broad human interaction experience into executable control.

Evaluation includes physical manipulation, held-out real-world instructions, three simulation benchmarks, and a qualitatively described visual-rollout interface. These establish different kinds of evidence and should not be combined into a single measure of world-model quality.

inputs: Task instruction, embodiment identity, and camera-view configuration
Packed multi-view observations and externally supplied robot states
Historical actions; candidate future action chunks in visual-simulation mode
During pretraining, video-derived latent actions or embodiment-specific trajectory labels
outputs: Continuous action chunks in the selected embodiment's control representation
Action-conditioned visual latents, decoded into RGB observations in simulator mode

steps.name: Standardize heterogeneous experience
steps.detail: The data engine creates instruction–observation–state–action trajectories. Human-video processing combines semantic segmentation, MANO hand reconstruction, camera-pose estimation, and quality filtering. Robot and handheld streams receive temporal alignment and action calibration. Per-embodiment normalization and validity masks preserve distinct physical action spaces; semantic-aware sampling addresses long-tail coverage.

steps.name: Encode a shared multimodal sequence
steps.detail: T5 encodes the structured prompt for cross-attention. A Wan VAE and 3D patch embedding encode the packed visual canvas. Embodiment IDs select category-specific state/action projections and action heads around a shared transformer. Clean history and noisy flow-matching targets occupy one sequence; action chunks align with visual-latent transitions.

steps.name: Enforce causal prediction dependencies
steps.detail: Actions depend on preceding visual, state, and action history; each subsequent visual latent additionally depends on the current action. Structured attention blocks access to future clean observations while permitting local within-block attention. Padding and invalid channel-step entries are excluded from losses and noise injection. Causality therefore concerns transition ordering, not strictly token-by-token attention inside every block.

training.text: Stage I first trains a latent-action VAE on adjacent frame pairs, then freezes it. Its 32-dimensional bottleneck supports next-frame reconstruction with weak KL regularization; posterior means become deterministic pseudo actions. Dense transition codes are grouped to match WAM action chunks. With action weight λ=0.1, this stage initializes dynamics rather than a deployable robot policy.

Stage II uses UMI, robot, and reconstructed human-hand trajectories with λ=0.5. Stage III excludes human and UMI data, retaining high-quality robot demonstrations with λ=0.9. Visual prediction remains an auxiliary training objective even when action prediction dominates.

Real-world post-training jointly adapts one generalist model to four tasks with λ=0.95. Section 4.2 reports three hours of teleoperation per task; Section 5.1.1 reports 15 demonstrations per task without explaining the relationship between those descriptions.

inference.text: Policy execution initializes a KV cache with the prompt, first observation latent, and initial state. The action head denoises Gaussian noise into a chunk, which is cached and executed for apf low-level steps. Returned observations and the final robot state supply clean context for the next chunk. Future-video generation is unnecessary in this loop.

Visual simulation accepts actions from the policy, a candidate plan, or a recorded trajectory. The latent head predicts their visual consequences and recursively conditions later predictions on generated observations. Robot states are not predicted: they must be observed or replayed. The interface therefore does not constitute a complete autonomous state simulator.

History is bounded by a fixed cache window. When full, the cache resets around the latest observation. This provides finite interaction memory; the paper does not specify the window length or measure the effects of resetting it.

equations.explanation: Equation (1): c is the task condition, z a visual latent, s an externally supplied state, and a an action chunk. The current action appears only in the visual-transition factor. Although later states enter the conditionals, the model generates no state-transition distribution.

equations.expression: x_σ = (1−σ)x + σε,  v* = ε−x;  L = (1−λ)L_z + λL_a.
equations.explanation: For visual latents or continuous actions x, Gaussian noise ε and noise level σ define the flow-matching regression target. Equations (2)–(3) apply squared velocity error with the different causal conditions above; Equation (4) combines the losses. λ changes across training stages, while validity masks exclude padding and invalid targets.

results.setting: Tianji Marvin dual-arm robot; joint post-training on ordered stacking, kitchen organization, clothes folding, and desk organization
results.metric: Average final-task SR and milestone-based PSR
results.comparison: G0.5: SR 70.00%; PSR 80.18%. The SR difference is 15.00 percentage points.
results.interpretation: These are reported physical-execution outcomes. Trial counts and uncertainty for this main four-task evaluation are not specified.

results.setting: Physical utensil storage, plate placement, and bowl stacking after task post-training
results.comparison: Best competing SR: G0.5 at 35.0%. Best competing PSR: LingBot-VLA at 80.2%.
results.interpretation: This is the largest highlighted task-level advantage, but the strongest comparator differs between the two metrics.

results.setting: Two held-out instruction tasks using seen object categories; 10 trials per task
results.metric: Task SR and two-task average SR
results.interpretation: The stricter instruction substantially reduces success. These small evaluations support task-specific transfer rather than unrestricted compositional competence.

results.setting: Objects, scenes, and goals absent from real-world post-training; no additional demonstrations or parameter updates; 10 trials per task
results.metric: Task SR and two-task average SR
results.value: Rubik's cube to storage box: 10/10; towel to basin: 7/10; average 85.0%
results.interpretation: These are executed robot trials. The stated holdout concerns post-training; exclusion from the large pretraining corpus is not established.

results.setting: Pretraining on 300 tasks followed by Target-50 fine-tuning; evaluation on 50 target tasks
results.comparison: ABot-M0.5 averages 54.2%; the average improvement is 8.4 percentage points.
results.interpretation: The strongest substantial simulation margin concerns compositional tasks under this adaptation protocol. Composite-Unseen should not be reinterpreted as an independently established zero-shot setting.

results.setting: 50 bimanual tasks; 50 clean and 500 randomized training demonstrations per task; Clean and Randomized evaluation
results.comparison: Section 5.2.2 reports the highest average among compared methods; concatenated leading table cells prevent a reliable numerical margin comparison here.
results.interpretation: This measures simulated task completion, not visual-rollout fidelity. Clean/Randomized component scores are omitted because of extraction ambiguity.

results.setting: Four official suites, each containing 10 tasks with 50 demonstrations per task
results.comparison: Being-H0.5 and G0.5 each have a legible reported average of 98.9%.
results.interpretation: The reported average lead is only 0.1 percentage points. Without uncertainty estimates, statistical separation is unresolved.

limitations.text: No mechanism-relevant ablations isolate action-first ordering, visual supervision, LAM initialization, curriculum stages, or semantic balancing. The reported gains therefore cannot be attributed separately to architecture, training schedule, or data scale.

Visual-simulator support consists of qualitative descriptions associated with Figure 10, whose images were not inspected. No quantitative prediction metric, counterfactual action-sensitivity test, or demonstrated planning improvement is reported.

Real-world PSR milestones are described conceptually but not specified sufficiently to reconstruct scoring. The main task suite lacks evaluation trial counts and uncertainty; held-out tasks use only 10 trials each.

The authors describe a common real-world setting, but matched pretraining data and compute across baselines are not established. DreamZero* is their separately trained reproduction, so its score should not be treated as an untouched official checkpoint result.
Efficient online control and long-horizon memory remain incompletely characterized: inference latency, denoising budget, and cache-window length are absent, and history is discarded at cache resets.

reproduction.text: A faithful implementation requires embodiment mappings, normalization statistics, camera packing, temporal alignment, validity masks, semantic sampling weights, and the curated source mixture. Section 2.1 reports more than 230K hours overall, including 200K+ human, 12K+ handheld/wearable, and 20K+ robot hours, but does not provide a fully reconstructable data manifest or sampling recipe.

The supplied paper leaves model size, optimizer settings, training steps, batch sizes, compute, exact sampling scheduler, and several preprocessing settings unspecified. The stated 5B model belongs to DreamZero*, not an established Riemann parameter count. No code was inspected and no experiments were reproduced for this report.

A useful small experiment would compare action-first and joint generation under matched backbone, data, and compute, measuring executed SR and latency. Separately, hold observation and state fixed while varying candidate actions to test visual responsiveness. These are proposed tests, not reported experiments.

reasoning.text: One Model is supported by explicit shared-transformer architecture evidence, despite embodiment-specific heads and a separate training-time LAM annotator. Other mechanisms/Outside quadrants fits the action-first autoregressive factorization: it neither generates actions by inverse dynamics from imagined futures nor requires simultaneous action–future denoising. The alignment subcategory fits progressive supervision and embodiment interfaces. Memory & long-horizon modeling has narrower support through cached interaction history and organization tasks; no dedicated memory ablation establishes its benefit.

discussionQuestions: How much does action-first ordering improve executed control under matched data and compute? [E03, E17]
Does the visual loss improve policy learning when future visuals are never generated during deployment? [E06, E07]
How can counterfactual visual rollouts remain consistent when future robot states are externally supplied rather than predicted? [E03, E16]
Which organization tasks depend on history lost during cache resets? [E07, E11]

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title, author block, and arXiv version line
evidence.detail: The supplied title, identifier, and all 16 named authors match the catalog. The observed version is arXiv:2608.27033v1, dated 27 August 2026.

The corpus includes 200K+ hours of human video, 12K+ handheld/wearable hours, and 20K+ robot hours. Processing standardizes action-level trajectories using semantic annotation, hand/camera reconstruction, alignment, normalization, validity masks, filtering, and semantic-aware sampling.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 7–8, Section 3.2, Equation (1) and adjacent paragraphs
evidence.detail: The action conditional precedes the visual conditional, which additionally receives the current action. States are externally observed or replayed, not generated. Policy mode uses actual observations; simulator mode recursively uses predicted visual latents.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 8–9, Section 3.2, input conditioning and embodiment-specific interfaces
evidence.detail: T5 supplies prompt embeddings, Wan VAE and patch embedding encode packed camera views, and embodiment IDs select state/action projections and action heads around a shared transformer backbone.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 9–10, Section 3.2, token alignment, causal attention, and loss masking
evidence.detail: Clean history and noisy targets share a sequence. Action chunks align with latent transitions; attention excludes unavailable future clean tokens. Validity masks remove padded or invalid targets, and inactive padded channels remain zero during noise injection.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, flow-matching preliminary; p. 10, Equations (2)–(4)
evidence.detail: The noise interpolation has target velocity ε−x. Separate latent and action velocity losses use their respective causal histories and combine as (1−λ)L_z+λL_a.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 10–11, Section 3.2, Autoregressive online inference
evidence.detail: The cache starts from text, initial observation, and state. A denoised action chunk executes for apf steps; actual observations and state update the cache. A full cache resets around the latest observation.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 11–13, Sections 4 and 4.1, Stage I and LAM objective
evidence.detail: A separately trained, frozen latent-action VAE supplies posterior-mean pseudo actions from adjacent frames through a 32-dimensional bottleneck. Stage I groups these into chunks and uses λ=0.1; the text explicitly excludes deployable-policy learning as its purpose.

evidence.location: PDF p. 13, Section 4.1, Stage II and Stage III
evidence.detail: Stage II combines UMI, robot, and annotated human-hand trajectories with λ=0.5. Stage III retains robot demonstrations only and raises λ to 0.9 while preserving visual supervision.

Post-training combines four tasks into one generalist model with action weight 0.95. Section 4.2 gives three hours per task; Section 5.1.1 gives 15 demonstrations per task and identifies the Tianji Marvin dual-arm robot.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 14–15, baseline setup, Table 1 average columns, and Section 5.1.2
evidence.detail: Riemann averages 85.00% SR and 94.43% PSR; G0.5 averages 70.00% and 80.18%. Kitchen scores are 90.0% SR and 98.4% PSR, versus best competing values of 35.0% SR and 80.2% PSR. DreamZero* denotes the authors' 5B reproduction.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 15 and 17–18, Section 5.1.3 and Table 2
evidence.detail: Each held-out task uses 10 robot trials. Riemann achieves 8/10 and 5/10 compositional successes, averaging 65.0%, and 10/10 and 7/10 OOD successes, averaging 85.0%. Comparator averages are 45.0%/15.0% and 50.0%/30.0%, respectively. OOD exclusion is defined against real-world post-training.
RoboCasa training uses 300 tasks followed by Target-50 fine-tuning. Riemann scores 74.2, 56.0, and 56.3 across the three groups, with reported average 62.6; ABot-M0.5 averages 54.2.

evidence.location: PDF p. 18, Section 5.2.2; p. 19, Table 4 headers
evidence.detail: RoboTwin training covers 50 tasks with 50 clean and 500 randomized demonstrations per task. Section 5.2.2 explicitly reports a highest average SR of 94.3%. Leading component-score cells in Table 4 are concatenated in the supplied extraction.

evidence.location: PDF p. 19, Section 5.2.3 and Table 5 Average column
evidence.detail: LIBERO uses four suites of 10 tasks with 50 demonstrations per task. Prose gives Riemann's suite scores as 99.6, 100.0, 97.6, and 98.6, with average 99.0. Being-H0.5 and G0.5 each have a legible average of 98.9.

Candidate or recorded actions condition visual-latent generation, and decoded or observed outputs can extend the context. The authors describe qualitative multi-embodiment rollouts associated with Figure 10; this section supplies no quantitative visual-fidelity, counterfactual-control, or planning-benefit evaluation.

The supplied training and experiment sections provide stage weights and benchmark outcomes but no mechanism ablation, Riemann parameter count, detailed optimizer/compute budget, inference timing, cache-window length, uncertainty estimates, or main four-task evaluation trial counts.
